title: Reflexivity
author: Nick Hart
summary: The premise here is that every leadership decision rests on interpretation, so leaders ought to interrogate why they think as they do. Hart separates reflexivity from reflection: reflection asks what happened and what was learned, while reflexivity asks how one's way of seeing shaped what was noticed, valued or ignored. To make this tractable he borrows three concepts from research methodology and applies each to school leadership. Ontology is illustrated through realist, relativist and positivist leaders, each of whom diagnoses a stalled set of outcomes differently and each of whom carries a characteristic blind spot. Epistemology is handled the same way, with Hart declaring his own interpretivist mix of early indicators, mapping of perspectives and headline measures, then contrasting positivist, constructivist and pragmatist stances. Positionality gets the most vivid treatment, including the claim that every school contains an imagined version living in dashboards and strategy documents and an experienced version living in corridors and classrooms, with seniority widening the gap between them. The practical counsel is to step in to connect and step back to make sense, and to keep asking whose voice is missing. Hart frames the whole exercise as the foundation of sense making.
points: The distinction between reflection and reflexivity is the piece's load-bearing move: one examines events, the other examines the lens that selected which events counted.

Hart's claim that truth does not rise to the top, because information loses nuance passing upward through layers of interpretation, is the strongest argument in the piece for leaders deliberately seeking disconfirming perspectives.
Each ontological stance is paired with its failure mode, so the realist overlooks human complexity, the relativist struggles to pin down action, and the positivist mistakes measurement for meaning.

Positionality is shown to extend well beyond job title, encompassing tenure in the community, prior experience of a failing school, and emotional attunement to tension before it shows in behaviour data.
The stated purpose of walking the building is diagnostic rather than supervisory: reflexive leaders walk to learn, on the understanding that perceived power distorts what people show them.
quotes: While reflection asks What happened and what did we learn?, reflexivity asks How did our way of seeing shape what we noticed, valued or ignored?

Reflexivity is noticing how our experiences, values and emotions shape what we pay attention to and what we ignore. It helps us to question the basis of our assumptions before turning them into action. Without it, we risk mistaking our own perspective for reality.
I see schools as complex adaptive systems, living networks of relationships where patterns emerge, feedback loops form and small changes can ripple unpredictably across the whole.
Two leaders can look at the same situation and reach different conclusions, not because they disagree about the facts, but because they hold different ideas about how truth is known.

Every school has at least two versions of itself; the imagined school that exists in our minds and is the best of our strategy documents, dashboards and presentations; and the experienced school that lives in classrooms, corridors and playgrounds.
When you are too close, it’s hard to see patterns; when you are too far away, it’s hard to feel the pulse. We might do better to step in to connect and step back to make sense.
The most effective leaders aren’t just thinking about their schools, they’re thinking about how they think about their schools.
